debris.notes: Curved skin plate off something that already burned once — the commonest thing in the low sky and the piece every player learns to latch on first.
A folded aluminium lattice that crushes down well; two slots of honest tonnage and the first piece that makes the jetpack feel heavy.
Interstage collar from a launcher that never made orbit — the heaviest hand-tetherable piece in the band, and a deliberate test of whether the player tows gently.
A balled-up wad of multi-layer foil: almost free to tow, but it still costs a full crushed slot, so it is the piece that teaches slot cost and mass are different currencies.
A composite wedge off a shattered payload fairing — light, plentiful, and the reliable filler that keeps a lazy run breaking even.
Star-cracked optical dome that still glints on a slow cycle; the player's first fragile piece, cheap enough to lose and instructive enough to matter.
A bent whip antenna on its feed block — the lightest fragile piece in the game, so a suborbital player can practise a gentle landing without much at stake.
A whole dead kick stage tumbling slowly; crane-cable only and therefore out of reach in the shipping slice, present so the oversized class exists in the lowest band the player ever flies.
The structural box a satellite was built around, stripped of everything soft — the low band's bread-and-butter haul and the first piece that visibly slows the ride home.

A folded array wing with half its cells starred, still carrying its full drive spine and hinge stack; never crushable, so it pays four uncrushed slots forever, and at a joint-heaviest 500 kg it is the archetypal fragile decision of the shipping slice — the most valuable thing in the band and the hardest to bring home intact.
A dense steel flywheel can — one slot of concentrated mass, which is what makes the low band heavier per slot than suborbital without filling the hold faster.
A punctured titanium sphere that crushes flat with a satisfying report; bulky before the compactor touches it, ordinary after.
A sealed inertial unit, solid and unglamorous — the piece a cautious player fills the last slot with when the shield plate is already low.

A quarter-segment of a comms dish, thin-skinned and awkward on the line; it spawns off the clumps and high in the band, so reaching it is a real burn — and at two uncrushed slots it is a fragile detour a nearly full hold can still say yes to.
A shaded optical head the size of a coffee can — the rarest thing in the low band and the cheapest fragile piece to tow, which makes the detour tempting rather than obvious.
An intact comsat body spinning end over end; crane-cable only, deferred with the crane magnet, and the rehearsal object for the capstone capture.
A potted flight-computer block, solid metal and boards all the way through — the high band's workhorse and, at half a tonne per slot, the reason a full hold up here needs extra passes.
A long array wing snapped mid-span, still glinting; the most frequently met fragile piece in the game and the one most often lost to a hot entry.
A strapped column of cells wrapped in shielding — one of three high-band pieces sitting at roughly a tonne, and the clearest single expression of 'the valuable stuff fights you'.
Four scorched attitude nozzles on a common manifold, crammed with precious metal; one crushed slot, and the densest thing per slot a hand magnet can hold.
A baffled tube with the primary mirror still seated — heavy, fragile, uncrushable, and the piece that makes a player choose between a soft landing and one more pass.
A frosted dewar off a science payload, thin-walled and unforgiving; small enough to slip into a nearly full hold, fragile enough to be the first thing a hard touchdown wrecks.
A foil-wrapped equipment bay torn cleanly off its bus — crushable, solid, and the safe high-band haul when the shield plate will not stand another hot pass.

A segmented mirror panel the size of a barn door: fragile and oversized at once, crane-cable only, deferred with the high band — it exists to preview the exact class Mr. Armstrong's satellite belongs to.

revision_notes: Finding 3 (cracked_solar_array is the lightest cargo per slot in its band) accepted, and it was the sharpest of the three. Mass goes 380 -> 500 kg, which is +32% and takes it from 95 kg per occupied slot to 125 — above the parabolic dish section's 120 and the star tracker's 105, so the band's fragile medium is now the heaviest of its fragile options rather than the lightest, which is the ordering a medium should have. I stopped at 500 rather than the suggested 600 for two reasons, one physical and one mechanical. Physical: 600 would make a folded array wing outweigh the satellite_bus_frame — a structural box stripped of everything soft — and the catalog stops reading as salvage the moment glass outweighs steel. Mechanical: 500 makes it joint-heaviest hand-tetherable in the band with the bus frame, so the worst two-tether low-band load rises from 950 to 1000 kg, a 5% give-back against the 1400 kg case the previous revision was routed here to fix. That is the largest raise available that does not undo the fix I was previously asked to make.

Finding 1 (iridium_battery_stack towing case) accepted in part: 1150 -> 1000 kg. The Balancer is right that this is a different number from the latch-shear case I declined last round, and the towing arithmetic is correct. What the trim actually buys, though, is less than the finding assumes, because the piece is not an outlier — dense_avionics_core is 1000 and gold_foil_bus_module is 980, so the worst two-tether high-band load only falls from 2300 to 2000 kg and base-tier EVA acceleration only rises from 0.214 to 0.244 m/s^2. Reaching the Balancer's 'noticeably heavier but still controllable' target from here means cutting the whole high-band medium population by roughly a third, which inverts the band mass gradient this catalog exists to hold (see design_notes). So I moved the piece to the top of its band's plateau instead of above it, and the remaining shortfall is the Jetpack upgrade's — the counterweight GDD 2.3.6 names for exactly this, and the tier a player is on by the time the high band is reachable. The Balancer's second option in that finding, a Jetpack tier gating the piece, is the right one and it is theirs to set.

Finding 2 (high band cannot be flown at full hold and full storage without landing damage) confirmed as deliberate, catalog unchanged. GDD 2.3.7 states it in as many words — 'difficulty scales with success automatically, and no thruster upgrade fully cancels it, because the player keeps filling the bigger hold' — and 2.3.6 makes Storage explicitly double-edged with the Parachute as its counterweight. The iridium trim moves the band from 500.7 to 485.1 kg per crushed slot, so the Balancer's 10-slot case lands at sqrt(2*6051*4/1628) = 5.45 m/s instead of 5.52: still over the line, which is the point. Note the shape of it, though — landing damage scales with velocity past 5 m/s, so 5.45 is a graze, not a wreck. Maximum greed at maximum storage costs a small tax rather than the haul, and the player can buy that ceiling back down by carrying nine slots instead of ten. That is a decision, which is what the design wants; if playtesting finds the tax reads as an unavoidable penalty rather than a choice, the lever is Storage t2's slot count or the Parachute curve, not the catalog.

No ids were added, removed or renamed, and nothing outside cracked_solar_array and iridium_battery_stack was touched. No spawn_weight changed, so all three fragile_fraction figures are carried unchanged and still verify: suborbital 9/87 = 0.103, low 12/67 = 0.179, high 14/56 = 0.250. Both mean_mass_kg rows that could move were recomputed from the final piece list: low 4460/8 = 557.5, high 8570/8 = 1071.25.
design_notes: Mass rises about 3.5x from suborbital to high on the plain per-piece mean (308.1 -> 557.5 -> 1071.3 kg), and about 4.3x if the crane-only oversized pieces are excluded (187.9 -> 351.4 -> 810.0 kg). That is the GDD 2.3.7 bet stated in numbers: the better the haul, the worse the ride home. This revision steepened the sub-to-low step slightly and flattened the low-to-high step slightly, both by design — the shipping slice needed the low band to pull harder, and the deferred band needed its ceiling to be a plateau rather than a single outlier piece.

The figure that actually reaches the physics is mass per crushed slot, because slots are what cap a hold. Suborbital runs ~103 kg/slot on crushable smalls and ~210 on mediums; low runs ~280 and ~238; high runs ~540 and ~497. A 6-slot starting hold therefore weighs roughly 0.6-1.3 t from suborbital, 1.4-1.7 t from low, and 3.0-3.2 t from high. Against the Researcher's 1400 kg staged ship that is beta 267 empty rising to ~385-505 from suborbital, ~535-590 from low and ~840-880 from the high band, i.e. two to three times the passes an empty ship needs. The catalog carries the band-to-band difficulty differential the Researcher warned entry speed alone could not (his note: only 1.35x flux from suborbital to high), which is exactly the beta lever he pointed at.

The high band's mediums are deliberately a plateau, not a peak: 980, 1000 and 1000 kg across gold_foil_bus_module, dense_avionics_core and iridium_battery_stack. That shape matters for tuning. When one piece is 15% clear of the field, the hand magnet's hold force and the jetpack's thrust get tuned against a single object and everything else feels slack; when three pieces sit within 2% of each other, the tuning target is the band, and any piece the player latches up there feels the same weight. It also means a mass complaint about the high band is a band-level finding by construction — trimming any one of the three moves the worst case by a few percent and nothing else.

Fragile cargo is structurally light per slot and that is the GDD's rule, not a catalog slip. A fragile piece can never be crushed, so it pays double slots at the same mass, which halves its kg-per-slot against any solid of the same size class. GDD 2.3.4 is explicit that 'fragility is bulk plus risk' — bulk and risk, not mass. So the low band's fragile options will always read light per slot (125, 120 and 105 kg/slot after this revision, against 238-280 for the solids), and the counterweight to a fragile hold being an easy ride home is that it is a fragile hold: double heat damage, double landing damage, and no compactor tier will ever help it. Raising fragile masses until they match solids on kg/slot would mean roughly doubling them, which makes glass outweigh steel and deletes the reason the flag exists. What was fixable — and is fixed — is the ordering within the fragile set: the medium should out-mass the smalls, and now it does.

Note that the low band is denser per slot on smalls (280 kg/slot) than on mediums (238 kg/slot). That inversion is deliberate and it is the band's identity: the reaction wheel housing and the gyro package are the pieces that make a low-band hold heavy, and they do it one slot at a time without filling the hold. So the low band's hold-limited weight and its tether-limited weight move independently, and a player who is struggling with the ride home has a real choice about which one to load.

Ship mass is not mine to set, and this is the one place the catalog constrains it. GDD 2.3.5 says a full hold at starting storage roughly doubles the rocket's mass; that holds here if the staged ship is around 1 t and the player is filling suborbital slots with mediums. If the crew prices the ship far below that, every mass in this catalog should be scaled by the same factor rather than re-authored piecewise — that instruction now applies to the EVA towing case as well, which is the only remaining open mass question and the one the Jetpack tiers should answer first.

The fragile gradient is spawn-weighted, not counted: suborbital 9/87 = 0.103, low 12/67 = 0.179, high 14/56 = 0.250. By piece count the three bands would read 2/8, 3/8 and 4/8 (0.25/0.375/0.50), which is why the fragile pieces carry the lowest weights in every band — a fragile piece has to be rare in encounter terms, not just rare in the type list.

No piece is strictly best, because mass and slot cost are deliberately decoupled. The insulation blanket wad is nearly free to tow and still costs a whole crushed slot; the platinum thruster cluster is one slot holding 540 kg. So the greedy choice at the tether is not the greedy choice at the hold, and the player has to decide which resource is scarce on this particular run.

Every size class and the fragile flag are all reachable inside the shipping slice. Suborbital and low hold five and four small pieces, two and three mediums, and two and three fragiles respectively, so nothing about the vocabulary waits on the deferred high band. The low band meets the fragile flag at both size classes — a cheap 2-slot detour in the dish section and star tracker, an expensive 4-slot commitment in the solar array — which is what makes fragility a judgement call rather than a single all-or-nothing question.

Oversized is one piece per band and nothing more: derelict upper stage, tumbling comsat core, mirrored survey array. All three are crane-cable only and expected to be unreachable this semester. The high band's is fragile on purpose, so the fragile-and-oversized class the win condition belongs to exists in the catalog before the satellite does.

Mr. Armstrong's satellite is deliberately not in this catalog. The Researcher puts it above the high band at ~360 km, and the charter asks for exactly three bands; it is a named capstone object, not a spawn-table entry, and pricing it as ordinary loot would be wrong.
